items.title: kajisho5/ffmpeg-skill
items.content:
Local video editor for coding agents: 42 FFmpeg tools with a machine-readable contract and an MCP server, for Claude Code, Cursor and Codex. Cut, captions, reframe, loudness, platform exports. No cloud, no API keys.

Give your coding agent a video editor. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any MCP client edits your footage with local FFmpeg, then checks its own output.

No cloud · No API keys · Python standard library

Left half is the input, right half is what the command produced. — all of it built by , so you can rebuild every frame of it yourself. The footage is synthetic (FFmpeg's own test sources) except in three demos, , and , which use two AI-generated clips of people who do not exist (demos/footage/).

is an Agent Skill for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and any agent that reads . It teaches the agent a fixed workflow (probe → edit losslessly where possible → check → verify) and ships that do the actual work with / : cut, join, silence removal, fit to duration and aspect, captions and karaoke, overlays and motion graphics, HDR → SDR and LUTs, audio clean-up and typed dynamics, sync with drift correction, multicam, loudness, delivery checks, whole-edit project rendering, batch folders. Every tool is also callable as an MCP tool ( advertises a core 12 by default to keep client context small, with listing all 42; every tool is reachable by name through either way), and the whole set is described by a machine-readable contract.

If and are on your PATH, it works: offline, on footage you would rather not upload.

(Self-Producing Execution Contract): each tool's — the part of its contract and MCP tool definition that has to track the CLI flag-for-flag — is never hand-authored beside the code. It is derived, at run time, from the same parser that already defines the CLI, and CI fails the build if any of it drifts. → full explanation

Standalone, and in an ecosystem

, this is a local FFmpeg engine: probe → edit → verify, and nothing else. No API key, no account, no other repo required. Everything above and below this section describes that standalone tool, and none of it changes if you never read the rest of this one.

In kajisho5's wider video-production ecosystem, this repo is the : it cuts, measures and exports files, and reports back in structured JSON. It does not decide what to cut, whether a deliverable is approvable, what makes a highlight interesting, or what a caption should say (the user's cue text is burned as written, never rewritten to fit) — those are a 's job, sitting in front of this engine, not inside it.

Cut / join / measure / export a file right now (), standalone
Put Remotion motion graphics (animated captions, silence jump cuts, audio-peak motion) on a real recording: its compositions take their length, fps, frame, silences, scene cuts, audio peaks and beats from this repo's , and . It verifies its render with and , composites a graphics layer with ( for its mode), and delivers through

An agent that "knows FFmpeg" still guesses: it assumes a frame rate, picks a codec the container cannot hold, re-encodes a file that only needed a stream copy, and reports "done" without opening the result. This skill takes the guessing out:

  • Every job starts with ; the agent decides from the measured duration, fps, resolution, colour and audio layout, not from the file name.
  • Structured tools, not shell strings. Each operation is a script with typed arguments. Nothing runs through a shell; no filter graph is accepted from the caller.
  • A contract the agent can read. states, for every tool, what it takes, what it writes, which FFmpeg components it needs and how the result is verified. The MCP surface is derived from it.
  • Verification after execution. The result is probed, checked against the destination's spec and, when the picture changed, looked at as a contact sheet.
  • No cloud, no API keys, no Python dependencies. Optional local transcription is used when a speech engine (Parakeet or a whisper) is installed, never required — by and, since 1.17, by (with , or since 3.6 with / ); both take a transcript you already have instead, and both refuse with the install lines rather than guessing. Both take and ; and set this machine's defaults (e.g. where that whisper.cpp model is installed; without either, auto and ). The engine runs on your machine and the audio is never uploaded; parakeet-mlx, faster-whisper and openai-whisper download their model weights the first time they run (parakeet-mlx's default from Hugging Face).

The design discipline behind this skill — per-operation verification for AI agents — is written up as a position paper. The paper scores ffmpeg-skill itself as only partially conformant with the discipline it defines.

# 0. FFmpeg itself, once (Ubuntu/Debian shown; macOS and Windows are in the Install table below)
sudo apt install ffmpeg

# 1. install the skill for Claude Code (Cursor: --cursor, Codex: --codex, all three: --all)
npx ffmpeg-skill

# 2. check the machine: ffmpeg, ffprobe and every FFmpeg component the tools need
npx ffmpeg-skill doctor

# 3. (for agent frameworks) read the machine-readable contract
npx ffmpeg-skill contract --json | head -40

Captions from speech () need one local speech engine, installed separately. pip install faster-whisper is the simplest; the first run downloads its model, and the audio never leaves the machine. Without an engine, everything else works, lists the engine as missing optional, and refuses with the install line for each engine it supports.

Already installed? re-run to refresh ~/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill. Copies are not updated automatically.

's overall and a single tool's are different signals: is false when anything tool requires is missing, so one missing filter (a plain Homebrew without , or a build without libvidstab) turns it false even though most tools still run. Check 's field for the per-tool answer, not just .

"Take , keep 0:45–3:10 and 5:00–6:30, and make it exactly 60 seconds for Reels."

The agent runs , cut.py --segments 0:45-3:10,5:00-6:30, fit.py --duration 60 --aspect 9:16 --fit crop, , check.py --platform reels and , then reports "final.mp4: 59.98 s, 1080×1920, 30 fps, AAC stereo" with the contact sheet it inspected.

One command per destination, with the app's own UI taken into account:

python3 $S/render.py talk.mp4 --template tiktok --cues cues.txt

That fills the shipped : 9:16 crop, captions popped word by word TikTok's description bar and clear of its like column, −14 LUFS, the export preset, and a check.py --platform tiktok on the file it wrote. The caption size comes from the delivery table, so since 1.17.1 the filled project also states : a size nobody asked for shrinks to fit the cue instead of splitting the sentence across two cues. A template that states its own , and a that states a caption size, still win, and a project with renders the captions 1.17.0 rendered. Templates ship for , , , , , , , , and ; (or a comma-separated list) renders the seven video destinations (, , , , , , ) from the same edit and writes a table of what each one produced. Files land next to the input unless says otherwise, and shows every planned command rather than a result. render.py --list-templates prints them with their frames, limits and safe zones. Alias spellings work everywhere a platform is named ( = , = , = , = ).

The tools also work on their own, from any shell:

S=~/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill/scripts
python3 $S/probe.py input.mp4 --compact
python3 $S/fit.py input.mp4 --duration 60 --aspect 9:16 --dry-run    # print the plan, run nothing
python3 $S/export.py input.mp4 --preset reels --json                 # structured result with a probe of the output

On Windows in Git Bash, is only on PATH if Python was installed from the Microsoft Store; a python.org install exposes (or the launcher) instead — replace with above if you see a "command not found". and / already handle this for you; only the raw script examples above need it spelled out manually.

More requests and the commands behind them: examples/README.md. To see everything run end-to-end on generated footage: (the gallery in docs/demos.md).

flowchart TD
    U[User request] --> A[AI agent<br/>Claude Code · Cursor · Codex]
    A -->|reads| S[SKILL.md<br/>workflow, request → tool map, report format]
    A -->|runs| T[Structured tool<br/>scripts/<name>.py, typed argparse flags]
    T --> C[Contract<br/>input schema · role · capabilities · verification policy]
    C --> D[Capability detection<br/>doctor: available / missing / unknown]
    D --> F[FFmpeg execution<br/>no shell, stream copy when possible]
    F --> V[Verification<br/>probe · check · look.py contact sheet]
    V --> R[Structured result<br/>--json: status, output, commands, probe]
    R --> A

Over MCP the same tools are reached through a transport that holds no tool table of its own:

flowchart LR
    M[MCP client<br/>Claude Desktop · Cursor · any client] --> P[mcp/server.py<br/>stdio JSON-RPC]
    P -->|tools/list| C[Contract-derived ToolSpecs<br/>names · order · inputSchema]
    P -->|tools/call| T[scripts/<name>.py]
    C -.derived from.-> K[scripts/_contract.py]
    T -.described by.-> K

Names, order and in are translated from each tool's argparse parser at start-up, so a new flag or a new script appears in MCP with no edit to . A test copies the skill, adds, removes and edits a script, and reads again to prove it.

These are the rules the skill file gives the agent and the code enforces.

  1. No tool decides from the file name. measures duration, fps (with variable-frame-rate detection), resolution, rotation, bit depth, HDR format including Dolby Vision, colour tags and every audio stream before anything is cut.
  2. and stream-copy what they do not need to touch ( re-encodes so it can crossfade and conform mismatched clips; joins clips that already match by stream copy). Re-encoding happens only when it must: frame-accurate cuts, filters, format changes, or a keyframe farther than the tolerance.
  3. Every tool takes (print the ffmpeg command lines, write nothing; ignores it), (the dry run saved as a plan with fingerprinted inputs that executes later, refusing if an input changed; and refuse it), (structured result with a probe of the output), (preview quality), (percent and ETA), (a hung ffmpeg is killed and reported, never waited on forever; Ctrl-C or SIGTERM likewise stops the running ffmpeg, removes its partial output and reports ) and (explicit consent before an existing output is replaced). A test runs every tool whose contract says its dry run runs no ffmpeg (, plus and without their measuring flags) under behind a fake ffmpeg and asserts that no ffmpeg call happened and no file appeared; another runs every tool the contract says supports (all but ) behind an ffmpeg that logs each decode, and asserts that no file appeared and that every tool that decoded is one the contract lists as .
  4. Machine-readable contract. describes all 42 tools: input schema generated from the parser, output schema, role, required and conditional FFmpeg capabilities, dry-run support, the verification tools to run afterwards, whether a visual check is required, . lists all 42 by a cross-repository Capability id (, , ...) for kajisho5/AI-video-production-OS's CapabilityContract.provides — see .
  5. builds its from the contract. Tool names, order and cannot drift from the scripts; a test keeps the two byte-identical.
  6. reads ffmpeg -encoders / -decoders / -filters / -bsfs and reports which of the components the tools need are present on this build (libx264, libass, zscale, loudnorm, xfade, …), before a job fails inside ffmpeg.
  7. When a listing cannot be read (a layout the parser does not know, ffmpeg exiting non-zero) the affected capabilities are : never , never silently . An installed filter is not reported absent; a failed detection is not a pass.
  8. The output is probed, and when the picture changed (captions, overlays, crops, colour, transitions) the agent runs and inspects the PNG. The report is not finished until its line names that image; audio-only jobs say . "Inspects" means the calling agent's own vision, not a feature of this skill: only renders a PNG; nothing in this repository detects faces, products, subjects, or "the interesting part" of a frame or a scene. When a crop or reframe needs to keep a specific part of the frame (fit.py --fit crop --crop-x/-y, see Tools), it is the multimodal agent looking at that PNG and choosing the anchor — a non-visual caller (a script, a CLI user without eyes on the sheet) has to supply that decision itself, and the default is a plain centre crop. Likewise ranks candidate scenes by a measured proxy ( or ), never by content; it is the agent that turns a look at the sheet into a judgement.
  9. A finished job is , a failure or a refusal is , and a partial result is with the shortfall named in — never a third label such as .
  10. No tool overwrites its input. Outputs are new files named <input>_<operation>.<ext> unless told otherwise, and a test hashes every input after the run.

42 public tools, all Python 3.10+ standard library, all with , , , (a dry run written as a plan executes later), non-zero exit and a reason on stderr on failure. (1.11.0) prints the same result document trimmed to what a caller acts on — status, output, , a compact of the output probe, the tool's own keys and the command count instead of the command lines — for roughly a third of the bytes; itself is unchanged. Every re-encoding tool except , and (a preset or the project decides there) takes --codec h264|hevc|av1|prores and (1.8) and, with , / (Apple VideoToolbox on Apple Silicon, opt-in; see below), and every time flag takes seconds, , or SMPTE with an optional suffix (1.9).

Duration, fps (+ VFR detection), resolution, codecs, bit depth, HDR format incl. Dolby Vision ( for a real PQ/HLG/DV transfer only, also for BT.2020 SDR), colour space, rotation, every audio stream; flags Log footage
Scene changes, audio peaks, highlight proposals ( loudest, or longest — both proxies, not "best") and a per-scene sheet; cut list for ; measures the music's beat grid (tempo, beat times, confidence); classifies each shot static/pan/motion by measured optical flow; lists per-second dBFS; reports a speech-vs-music ratio, not a classification
Contact sheet, single frames, side-by-side comparison as PNG so the agent can see what it made; shades the zones a platform's own UI covers; --guides title,action,4:3 outlines the broadcast safe areas (on the PNG only)
In/out or multi-segment cuts, lossless first, re-encode fallback, for frame-exact video and sample-exact audio, for a frame-exact H.264 cut that re-encodes only the partial GOPs at the cut points (matched to the source, verified against its packets and frames) and copies the rest, an SDR HEVC source re-encodes as HEVC ( for x264), a single / copy keeps its edit list, so the picture starts at unless a keyframe lands later ( then says so; for 2.x's shifted start), to choose the VFR check ( by default); reports ; moves the in/out points onto a measured beat, or refuses when there is no measurable pulse ; drops ranges and keeps the rest
Concatenate clips with xfade transitions, normalising size, fps, sample rate and channel layout (the widest clip's, or ); audio-only inputs are joined as audio; reads generated segments (TTS lines) and checks every one first — missing, empty or unreadable parts are all named in one refusal, or skipped and reported with ; joins clips with matching streams by stream copy, measured afterwards, and refuses a mismatch by name
Detect and remove dead air (jump cuts) with a margin around speech (, 0.2 s each side); list or export the cut list, or a source-to-output time map (, JSON or CSV); reports the level at every cut and warns where one may land in a breath or a word's tail; also removes filler words, but only where a speech engine timed them; keeps a breath inside a sentence and cuts only at sentence-boundary pauses, composing with through the same ; / keep different amounts before and after speech, and with word timings / give the pause after a sentence end (the transcript's punctuation) its own floor and tail
Fit to a duration (pitch-preserving speed change or trim, smooth slow-mo) and/or aspect ratio (pad, crop or 's blurred, darkened fill, with / to keep an off-centre subject) and/or exact /, with the result's saying where the picture sits in the frame written (measured); rotate 90/180/270, flip h/v; force constant fps
Crop to an exact pixel rectangle () — distinct from , which crops to an aspect ratio it computes itself
Measure existing black letterbox/pillarbox bars and report the -ready rectangle that removes them — analysis only, writes no file; reports the per-second motion centroid instead, for a 9:16 reframe — report only, the calling agent picks the crop, no auto-reframing
Deinterlace interlaced source footage (), /,
Reduce video noise/grain (), --strength low/medium/high or individual spatial/temporal overrides
Blur, pixelate, or () interpolate away an exact pixel rectangle for the whole clip. The box is given: nothing here finds a face, a plate or a logo, and is a border blend, not inpainting
Extract a flat rectilinear viewport from a 360/spherical video (--yaw --pitch --roll --h-fov --v-fov); no subject tracking, only the aim you give it
Rotate by an arbitrary angle for horizon correction (, ) — distinct from 's exact 90-degree turns
Turn a still image into a silent, fixed-duration video clip (title card, end slate) at an exact frame size / fps, with an optional Ken Burns zoom/pan
Generate a solid-colour or two-colour gradient clip at an exact size/duration — no input file; writes a fully transparent canvas (ProRes 4444, QuickTime Animation, PNG or VP9 with alpha) to draw graphics on
Reverse playback (video and, unless , audio)
Two-pass motion stabilisation (/)
Numbered () or glob-matched still images into a video
Render an audio track as a waveform or spectrum visualization video (/) — for audio-only inputs with no picture worth showing; puts the visualisation over a still plate (an audiogram), with , and burnt-in captions
Hold a frame for N seconds (, , ) — an end-card hold or a comedic beat
Add black/silent padding at the start and/or end of the timeline (, ) — distinct from 's per-frame letterbox bars
Step through different constant speeds across a clip via --segment START-END:FACTOR (repeatable) — distinct from 's single whole-clip speed factor
Repeat a clip N or to a target — for background loops and filling a fixed slot length; smooths the seam, plays it forward then backward
Cut away to a B-roll clip over the A-roll for a window (--insert B --at T --duration D, repeatable) and come back; A's length and audio untouched by default
Write container chapter markers from a text file and title/artist/comment tags, every stream copied bit for bit; proposes the markers from measured pauses and scene cuts and names them for you to rename
Composite x clips into one grid, each cell letterboxed and labelled with its filename by default ( to skip)
Voice clean-up chain at three strengths (--voice light|medium|strong), FFT denoise, typed compressor / limiter / gate, music bed with sidechain ducking (--duck-amount/-threshold/-attack/-release), a never-ducked effects bed (), , fades, 5.1 → stereo, track replacement, extraction (), , a tempo change that keeps the pitch (, atempo stages in 0.5–2.0) and an exact length in samples (), resampling () and one channel by index (), each read back from the output
Offset between two recordings by audio cross-correlation (1 ms, pure Python), clock-drift correction; aligned video or audio out (audio-to-audio only — no lip-sync/face detection); a third or later camera is an additional positional (), the positional itself keeps its name
Two-pass EBU R128 to −14 LUFS / −1 dBTP or any target ( for the range), video stream-copied; the written file is measured again and re-encoded until it meets (lossy encoders overshoot); ; --versions streaming,ebu-r128,broadcast-jp (or pairs) writes one file per target from one master, each measured after and listed in ( is null), only when every version met its own target
Burn SRT/ASS with font, size, colour, outline, position; build SRT from timed plain text; wraps to the safe area — with , the destination's own left/right safe zone, which since 1.17.2 is also what the burnt ASS states as its side margins — with a phrase-aware breaker () and //; takes a repeated for several language-tagged, toggleable tracks in one file; picks a font by script for non-Latin text (); animated and word-by-word karaoke timed to the speech energy or real word timings; shrinks the size until a cue fits instead of splitting the sentence (on by default on the delivery-template path since 1.17.1, where the size comes from the platform table); says when it burned the cues exactly as given; optional local transcription
Logos, watermarks and titles with position, time range, opacity, fades; keeps them clear of that destination's UI; for picture-in-picture, for green-screen compositing, to lay ranges of a layer at chosen times; composites onto a transparent canvas or alpha clip and writes the result with its alpha; a VP9 layer with alpha keeps its transparency
Lower-thirds, title cards, chapter chips, progress bars, countdowns, corner bugs, social stickers, opening hook cards and meme captions drawn by FFmpeg from a brand kit; keeps them inside that destination's safe zone; routes shaping scripts through libass and composites colour emoji; renders a template on a transparent canvas as a per-element alpha layer
HDR10 / HLG / Dolby Vision → SDR BT.709 tone mapping, DV layer stripping, 3D LUT (.cube), colour-tag rewriting, typed primary correction (exposure/contrast/saturation/gamma/white balance/lift-gain/levels/curves); grades an alpha clip and keeps its alpha, checked frame by frame; --legalize bt709|ebu-r103: a legal-range clamp after the 4:2:0 conversion, measured on the written file
Presets , , , , , , , , (HEVC Main10, source HDR tags kept), , , ////, the alpha masters //// (alpha read back), (a switcher's fill + key pair), , , , all tagged BT.709 unless they carry HDR or are an editing master (, : the source's tags kept, codec, profile and pixel format read back) (a BT.601-matrix or RGB source is converted to BT.709, not relabelled); meets the platform's loudness in the same call ( turns it on by default for platform presets) ; fits the file under a size limit by a two-pass encode and measures it ; remuxes a damaged file (timestamps regenerated, corrupt packets dropped) and counts the errors before and after
Small, low-bitrate proxy for downstream AI analysis/preview/editing decisions — resize by /, proxy-grade (default 30), , ; not a delivery preset

Gotchas and best practices

The short list for humans. The agent-facing version, with the reasoning, is the "Things that look right but are wrong" and "Gotchas" sections of SKILL.md.

  • Variable frame rate (phone and screen recordings). flags it; every re-encoding tool conforms to a constant rate automatically. samples the frame timing before a copy and switches to frame-accurate mode when it is variable or too short to judge, because copy-cuts on VFR land on the wrong frame ( restores 2.x's rule, re-encoding whenever the nominal and average rates differ; keeps the copy). Choose the rate yourself with fit.py input.mp4 --fps 30 when the measured average is odd.
  • Lossless cuts snap to keyframes. A stream-copy cut can start up to one GOP earlier than asked. re-encodes when the snap exceeds 0.5 s ( changes the limit). For a strictly lossless file pass (plus on a variable-frame-rate source), and expect the cut to land on the nearest earlier keyframe; the JSON result lists them under . A join can still be re-cut: open-GOP video, a later segment of B-frame / video that starts between keyframes (start it on a keyframe, or write ), or a join that fails its check. A single / copy keeps its edit list by default (since 3.0.0), so the picture starts where asked: the keyframe's pre-roll is stored but hidden by an MP4 edit list, which a player that ignores edit lists shows ( starts the file at the keyframe instead).
  • Frame-exact without re-encoding the whole cut (H.264). re-encodes only from each cut point to the next keyframe and copies the GOPs between, matched to the source's profile, level, pixel format, B-frame depth and colour tags. It checks the result against the source (frame grid, copied packets, decoded frames). A source it cannot match (HEVC, 10-bit, interlaced, VFR, open GOPs) is re-encoded in full, and says why. probe.py --keyframes-near T shows where the keyframes are.
  • When the probe reports HDR (HDR10, HLG, Dolby Vision, BT.2020), the tools keep it rather than flatten it. Convert deliberately with before H.264 deliverables or LUT work. platform presets are SDR and warn on HDR input.
  • −14 LUFS / −1 dBTP for YouTube and social platforms (the default), for podcasts, for broadcast. A clip measured at −40 LUFS or below is room tone, not content; raising it raises the noise. Check true peak as well as LUFS: check.py file --platform podcast measures both.
  • Alpha is kept only when asked, and a lost alpha is not verified. The re-encoding tools write opaque H.264 by default. On a source whose alpha is used (ProRes 4444, QuickTime Animation, PNG, VP9 with alpha), , and take (ProRes 4444 by default, --alpha-codec qtrle|png|vp9, --alpha-mode straight|premultiplied) and read the alpha back; without it the result says with a failing step, and records that an opaque output is wanted. background.py --transparent makes the canvas to draw graphics on.
  • Broadcast legal levels are measured, not assumed.check.py final.mxf --levels ebu-r103 (or ) counts every luma and chroma sample outside the legal range and FAILs when one frame has more than 1 % out (); the JSON adds min/max Y/U/V per . color.py --correct --legalize ebu-r103 clamps after the 4:2:0 conversion and measures what the encode left: a lossy encoder can push a few samples around a clamped edge back out, so the result says how many.
  • Frame changes first, text second. Captions and overlays burned before a crop or resize end up off-frame. Reframe, then caption.
  • Cropping 16:9 to 9:16 discards 70 % of the width. centres by default; pass / toward the subject, or pad with --fit pad --pad-fill blur. Look at the contact sheet before deciding.
  • Phrase-aware caption breaking (1.16)./graphics.py --wrap phrase (the default) never breaks inside a word or on the wrong side of a hyphen, never leaves a lone digit, kana or punctuation pair on a line, prefers Japanese sentence ends and particles over a mid-word break, and never ends a line on an article or preposition. All four are penalties over break positions that already fit, so no line is widened and the line count never changes; restores 1.15's width-only wrap. The text itself is never rewritten or shortened. Since 1.16.1 a Thai run and a katakana word are never broken inside (Thai writes no space inside a phrase and there is no dictionary: the break goes where you put a space or ), and a line wider than the safe width is reported as with the fix named.
  • Caption size fitted to the cue (1.17, reachable from the templates since 1.17.1). At a platform caption size a line holds about six em, so an ordinary sentence needs four lines and used to cut it into consecutive cues — half the sentence arriving late. (default ) walks the size down until every cue fits, laying the cues out, with a legibility floor of 4.5 % of the frame height (, default 13 ASS units). An explicit or a size is a statement about the look and is never overridden — which in 1.17.0 also silenced the fitter on every run, since a template fills the size from the platform table; 1.17.1 marks that size as the default it is ( in the filled project), so the type shrinks and no cue is split. restores that earlier behaviour byte for byte, and the caption text is still never rewritten to make it fit.
  • reports the measured grid — tempo, beat times, and a confidence built from how far the winning autocorrelation lag stands above the others and how many onsets land on it. (and a block in a project) moves in/out points to the nearest beat within — and only onto the grid points a measured onset actually marks, never onto the regular grid's continuation through a passage with no music in it. Below it : a cut point may move to a measured beat and may not appear from one, so speech and ambience get an honest "no steady pulse here" instead of an invented grid. A music bed is measured as it is delivered, WAV/FLAC/MP3 with no picture; on a synthetic click track at 90 and 120 BPM every beat is within 1 ms (WAV/FLAC) or 9 ms (MP3) of its click, holds it to 20 ms.

Can I pass raw ffmpeg arguments, or a filter_complex?

Each operation is a script whose flags are its argparse parser, and that parser is what and the MCP are built from. CI fails the build when those drift from the scripts. A caller-supplied filter graph, string, or other ffmpeg option is not an argument any script accepts. reads (and , ) and reports a filter a tool needs before a job runs into it. MCP does accept an array, and that array is the named script's own CLI flags, still bound to that script: the script's flags, never an ffmpeg command line and never a shell.

Why 42 tools? Isn't that overkill?

One tool per job, because each job promises something different, and the tool measures that promise after the run. re-measures integrated loudness and true peak. reports how far a cut snapped to a keyframe. returns the ranges it kept. checks the preset's maximum length. A value a tool cannot read fails that step as ; it does not pass. One tool with a mode flag would need as large a schema, and its checks would be vaguer.

An agent does not read 42 schemas. Over MCP, advertises the core 12 (bold below). The other 30 are called by name through when a job needs one, and lists all 42. The groups are the ones in Tools.

In the 100-prompt agent eval (1.17.0, Tested on real footage) the agent made no raw ffmpeg calls and reported no false successes.

How does ffmpeg-skill compare with Remotion?

ffmpeg-skill edits footage you already have, on this machine, with FFmpeg tools whose flags are a machine-readable contract (). Remotion renders a video from React components. They complement each other: this repository does not call Remotion, and a file Remotion writes is an ordinary input (, , , , ). joins the two. It measures the footage with this repo, draws the graphics in Remotion from those measurements, and checks and delivers the result with this repo again. Install both (, then npx remotion-ffmpeg-skill). As with the other skills, the dependency runs one way: it calls these tools, and nothing here calls it. HyperFrames renders a video from HTML and is the same kind of neighbour: a file it writes is an ordinary input too.

Does it validate the filter graph before running?

No. prints the ffmpeg command a writing tool would run and does not start ffmpeg, so ffmpeg never parses that filter graph. ffprobe still runs when the tool probes an input that exists. Unless is passed, an existing output is refused () before ffmpeg. An output that is the same file as an input is refused either way. No media file is written, and is false; does write the plan JSON. A path that is not on disk yet is not measured: the probe is a stub (0×0, duration 0), so a number taken from it is not a measurement. A plan is not a promise of the outcome: 's plan of a stream copy names in what a real run may still re-encode it for (: where the copy lands is measured from the written file). A real run starts with its own dry run, so when that dry run is refused because a stage needs a filter or an encoder the build lacks, the real run is refused the same way before the first stage encodes. Can it remove burned-in subtitles or logos?

A rectangle you already know, sitting still for the whole clip, can be filled from the picture around it with (ffmpeg's filter). That is a 1 px border blend. It is not inpainting: a logo that moves, or burned-in subtitles whose position changes, is out of scope. The same known box can be obscured instead, with or . None of the three finds the box. also needs the box at least 1 px inside the frame, and it only interpolates 8-bit YUV, so an HDR or 10-bit source is refused until .

Does it auto-track faces or subjects for reframing?

centres the crop unless you pass and . cuts the rectangle you pass. measures letterbox bars, and reports where motion sat each second; it writes no file and picks no crop. points a 360 view where you aim it. writes a contact sheet. Nothing in this repository detects a face, a product or a subject. Choosing what to keep in frame is the caller's.

Does it encode on the GPU?

The encode path a tool will actually take is Apple VideoToolbox, for h264, hevc and prores, and only on Apple Silicon. asks for it on that call. makes it the default for every re-encoding tool except 's delivery presets, which take on their own (or for a whole project). AV1 stays on SVT-AV1. nvenc, QSV, VAAPI and AMF are reported by 's when the ffmpeg build was compiled with them, and no tool encodes with them. One build is the exception to opt-in: with no and no , and with or , those encodes use VideoToolbox without and the result says is . still asks for the CPU encoder. A VideoToolbox job the hardware refuses is re-encoded on the CPU and the result says so ().

With no on at all, or to make the whole shell use it, do one of two things:

's own introspection calls (///) time out after 10s and report rather than hanging forever — those are meant to be fast. Every tool's actual media-processing invocation (cut, fit, caption, ...) runs under (default 1800 s, , = none): past the limit the process is killed, its partial output removed, and the failure reported as (exit 124) — a legitimately long re-encode should raise the limit rather than run unbounded. is always passed, so a hung ffmpeg process waiting on stdin cannot happen.

3.x keeps every tool name, CLI argument, JSON output key and exit code working: nothing is removed or renamed, and nothing optional becomes required, until 4.0. The full list of what is promised and what is not, and the three-step deprecation policy, is in docs/contract.md. It is enforced by a test that pins every tool's argument names against a snapshot, so a breaking change fails CI instead of slipping into a patch. Releases are batched: related fixes and features ship together as one version rather than one version per merged pull request, so a dependent project sees fewer, larger steps. Pin a tagged version, not . 2.0.0 made the five changes announced since 1.10.0 -- removed in favour of (except on , whose preset chooses the encoder), an existing output refused without , 's narrowed to a real HDR signal, / out of the MCP schema, the preview withdrawn -- listed with what to change in docs/contract.md and under in . 3.0.0 is the second break: it removed FFmpeg 5.x and Python 3.9 (announced in 2.14.0 and 2.10.9), made keep an / copy's edit list, keep an SDR HEVC source HEVC and use by default (, and restore 2.x), and changed what 's (now the least exact segment's) and (now equal to ) mean ( 2.0) -- see docs/contract.md.

npm test                      # tests/run_parallel.py (test_all.py's end-to-end modules, sharded across the cores) + tests/test_contract.py
python3 tests/test_picture.py # one tool group on its own (analysis, editing, cut_copy, audio, picture, delivery, orchestration, accel, asr)
npm run release-check         # pack, install, contract from the installed copy, MCP == contract, doctor, tests, contract evals
npm run demo                  # python3 demos/build.py: synthetic footage (and two AI-generated clips) -> every before/after demo + docs/demos/*.gif
npm run demo:pipeline         # examples/make_demo.sh: the older single end-to-end run, one clip through 13 of the 42 scripts
python3 evals/run.py --list   # agent eval prompts (see evals/); regex-only grading, runnable from any agent harness -- see evals/README.md "Running this from Cursor, Codex, or another harness"
node bin/install.js --dir /tmp/skills   # try the installer without touching ~/.claude

CI () runs on every pull request and on pushes to , on Ubuntu (FFmpeg 6.1 with Python 3.10 on 24.04, FFmpeg 8.0.1 with Python 3.13 on 26.04), macOS (Homebrew FFmpeg 8.x) and Windows (gyan.dev FFmpeg 9.x), plus a Linux job on FFmpeg 7.1 (Debian trixie container), and uploads each runner's FFmpeg listings as an artifact.

runs on all three OSes, but some of its tests put a fake or (a script on a PATH shim) in front of the real one — to record every call under , to force specific FFmpeg 6/7/8/9 fixture layouts through 's parser, to report an old version, to hang or fail on cue — or need what Windows does not have or does differently (SIGTERM, unprivileged symlinks, a line break or a backslash in a file name). Those tests, among them test_dry_run_never_runs_ffmpeg_and_writes_nothing and the whole class, skip there (, or inside the test) and show as , not silently absent, in the Windows job's log; grep -n 'os.name == "nt"\|platform.system() == "Windows"' tests/test_contract.py finds their conditions, among the suite's other platform branches. The rest — contract schema, , , MCP derivation, and the tools exercised through the contract, including 's provenance fields — runs against the real Windows on every PR. See references/ci-platform-pitfalls.md for this and other per-OS behaviour differences already diagnosed, before spending a CI cycle re-diagnosing a platform-only failure.

is fully automated end to end, including the version number itself — a PR never needs to touch or the version in . is different: the release writes the version heading and one line per merged PR, but a PR writes its own notes under (CONTRIBUTING.md), and a PR that closes an issue must name that issue in or test_changelog_mentions_every_closed_issue_since_last_tag fails. Once a PR merges to , .github/workflows/release.yml takes it from there: if nobody bumped the version by hand, it resolves the next version (.github/scripts/resolve_version.py) from the labels on every PR merged since the last tag (// → minor, // → patch, an unlabeled PR defaults to ; a PR whose only labels are , , or is not releasable, so a merge that changes no shipped file releases nothing). Most PRs don't need a label added by hand: 's job applies one automatically from the PR's title/changed files ( → , / → , /// changes → ) as soon as it's opened — add a label yourself only to override that. A major version is never chosen automatically: no label rule produces , and the workflow refuses to auto-bump across a major boundary even if someone applies that label — a real major release is a deliberate bump in a PR, which the manual path below already handles. It bumps , .claude-plugin/plugin.json, and 's released-version sentence, writes a section listing those PRs (and any issues they closed), and pushes that commit to itself. If another PR merged while the bump was being prepared, the push is refused and that run releases nothing: the newer merge's own run, queued behind it, starts from 's tip and releases both (the bump is never rebased onto a merge it did not read). After the tag it also asks to rebuild the site, because the bump commit carries and would otherwise leave the site on the previous version. Either way — auto-bumped or hand-bumped in the PR — it then creates the tag, publishes a GitHub Release with notes extracted from 's matching section, and publishes the package to npm. A PR that still wants to write its own version bump and prose (e.g. to explain the "why" of a release by hand) can — the automation only fills in when nobody made that call already. A push to with nothing new to release creates no tag, Release or npm publish; its MCP Registry step still asks npm and the registry about 's version and publishes the entry only when npm has that version and the registry does not, which is how a later run finishes an entry an earlier one failed to publish. npm publishing needs an repo secret (an npm access token with publish rights on this package) — without it the tag and GitHub Release still happen, only the npm step is skipped. A repo that depends on this one (an editing skill, an agent) should pin an version by tag or npm version, not by tracking — a merged-but-not-yet-released commit on can be ahead of the last published npm version for the few minutes between merge and this workflow completing.

A version that was tagged but never reached npm (the npm step failed; a re-run of that release sees the tag and skips the publish) is finished by dispatching the same workflow on its tag: gh workflow run release.yml --ref vX.Y.Z -f version=X.Y.Z. That runs only the workflow's job. It refuses a version that is not , has no tag, or that npm already has, and a run whose commit is not the tagged one: the npm provenance attestation names the run's commit, so it must be the commit the package is built from. It publishes with under the dist-tag when the version is above every stable (non-prerelease) version npm has, and under otherwise, so never moves back. Then it publishes the branch when no commit there is for this version and the branch's tip is older, and the MCP Registry entry when the registry does not list the version (never for a ). The GitHub Release is left as it is. A tag cut before the job was added (#448; every tag up to v3.6.3) has no job at its commit and cannot be recovered this way.

the release history from 1.8.0, one theme per minor, each marked shipped + evaluated, shipped with eval pending, or planned; and what 2.0.0 then removes
behaviours that look like bugs but are decisions, with rationale and the pinning test; read before filing a bug
what the agent reads: workflow, request → tool map, audio-only rules, report format, pitfalls
process mistakes already made once (breaking a pinned test by narrowing a capability list, retrying a git/GitHub operation this environment can't do, re-designing a fixture instead of recognising a real platform difference) — a living record, add to it whenever one recurs
the execution contract field by field, MCP relationship, how a planner consumes it
natural-language requests and the commands behind them, , , batch recipes

If this skill saves you time, you can help keep it maintained through GitHub Sponsors. Issues and pull requests are just as welcome.

items.title: google-research/paper-orchestra
items.content:
PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing.

Yiwen Song , Yale Song , Tomas Pfister , and Jinsung Yoon
Google Cloud AI Research

PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing. It flexibly transforms unconstrained pre-writing materials (ideas and experimental logs) into submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts, including comprehensive literature synthesis and generated visuals, such as plots and conceptual diagrams.

Acting like an orchestrated team of specialized agents, it handles outline generation, literature review, section writing, content refinement, and plotting to close the gap between raw research materials and submission ready papers.

  • : Orchestrates specialized agents (Outline, Literature Review, Section Writing, Content Refinement, Plotting) for end-to-end paper generation.
  • Comprehensive Literature Synthesis: Automatically searches, prioritizes, and integrates relevant literature into the manuscript.
  • : Generates plots and supports the inclusion of conceptual diagrams.
  • : Produces submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts adhering to target conference templates.

  1. : The project relies on a Conda environment named . You can set up a similar environment with Python 3.11 and install the required dependencies.

    conda create -n paper_orchestra python=3.11
conda activate paper_orchestra
pip install -r requirements.txt

  2. : Create a file in the root of the project and add your API keys:

    # Add keys if you have them, otherwise leave them empty
# You need to specify related keys if you want to use the model
# For example, if you want to use Gemini models, you need to specify either VERTEX_AI_PROJECT and VERTEX_AI_LOCATION, or GEMINI_API_KEY
# If you want to use OpenAI models, you need to specify OPENAI_API_KEY

SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY=your_semantic_scholar_api_key
OPENAI_API_KEY=your_openai_api_key
VERTEX_AI_PROJECT=your_vertex_ai_project
VERTEX_AI_LOCATION=your_vertex_ai_location
GEMINI_API_KEY=your_gemini_api_key

# if you want to run demo and send emails to yourself at the end, set these 2 fields as well
SMTP_EMAIL=your_email
SMTP_PASSWORD=your_password

The dataset used for paper generation is in this code repository. It will be released separately at a later date. Once available, you should download the dataset and place it under the directory.

You can run the paper generation pipeline using the provided bash script or directly via the Python CLI.

Using the Python CLI directly

python paper_writing_cli.py \
  --raw_materials_dir /path_to_your_raw_materials/ \
  --latex_template_dir /path_to_your_latex_template/ \
  --output_dir /path_to_your_output_folder/ \
  --use_plotting true
  • : (Required) Directory containing the raw materials (e.g., idea and experimental log).
  • : (Required) Directory containing the LaTeX template (e.g., ).
  • : Directory to output the generated paper. If not specified, an automatic folder with a timestamp is created.
  • : Enable the plotting agent workflow to generate figures from code (Default: ).
  • : LLM for writer and literature agents.
  • : LLM for reflection agents.

We provide an interactive Streamlit demo for the paper generation pipeline. For instructions on how to run and use it, please refer to the README.md in the directory.

  • : Contains scripts for automated evaluation.
  • : Core logic for agents and pipeline execution.
  • : LaTeX templates for target conferences, you can add your own template by creating a new subfolder under this directory.
  • : Utility functions for API calls, PDF handling, etc.

If you find this repo or our paper helpful, please cite it as follows:

@article{song2026paperorchestra,
  title={PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing},
  author={Song, Yiwen and Song, Yale and Pfister, Tomas and Yoon, Jinsung},
  journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.05018},
  year={2026}
}

This is not an officially supported Google product.

items.title: mvanhorn/last30days-skill
items.content:
AI agent skill that researches any topic across Reddit, X, YouTube, HN, Polymarket, and the web - then synthesizes a grounded summary

An AI agent-led search engine scored by upvotes, likes, and real money - not editors.

This README tracks the current v4 pipeline. The runtime skill spec lives in skills/last30days/SKILL.md, which is the source of truth for the latest command and setup behavior.

Claude Code (recommended — auto-updates via marketplace):

/plugin marketplace add mvanhorn/last30days-skill
/plugin install last30days

Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI, or any of 50+ Agent Skills hosts:

npx skills add mvanhorn/last30days-skill -g

( installs globally for your user, available across all projects. Drop it to scope per-project.)

More install options (claude.ai web, OpenClaw, manual) in the Install section below.

Zero config. Reddit, HN, Polymarket, and GitHub work immediately, and so do patent filings and careers pages when your topic is a company. Run it once and the setup wizard unlocks X, YouTube, TikTok, arXiv, Techmeme, and more in 30 seconds.

Reddit upvotes. X likes. YouTube transcripts. TikTok engagement. Polymarket odds backed by real money and insider information. That's millions of people voting with their attention and their wallets every day. /last30days searches all of it in parallel, scores it by what real people actually engage with, and an AI agent judge synthesizes it into one brief.

Google aggregates editors. /last30days searches people.

You can't get this search anywhere else because no single AI has access to all of it. Google search doesn't touch Reddit comments or X posts. ChatGPT has a deal with Reddit but can't search X or TikTok. Gemini has YouTube but not Reddit. Claude has none of them natively. Each platform is a walled garden with its own API, its own tokens, its own auth. But you can bring your own keys and browser sessions, and suddenly an AI agent can search all of them at once, score them against each other, and tell you what actually matters.

That's the unlock. Not one better search engine. A dozen disconnected platforms, bridged by an agent.

/last30days Peter Steinberger

You have a meeting tomorrow. You Google them. You get their LinkedIn from 2023. /last30days gives you what they're actually doing this month: joined OpenAI to work on Codex, fighting Anthropic's ban on third-party agents, shipping 23 PRs at 85% merge rate, building "LobsterOS" for cross-device agent control, and r/ClaudeCode hit 569 upvotes debating whether he's a hero or "insufferable." Scattered across X posts, Reddit threads, YouTube transcripts, and GitHub commits. None of it was on Google.

I built it to keep up in AI. Everything changes every day and the Reddit and X nerds are always on top of it first. I needed better prompts, and the training data was always months behind what the community had already figured out.

But it turned into something bigger. Now I run it before a sales call to know the last 30 days truth about a business. Before a meeting to read someone's recent tweets and podcast transcripts. Before a Disney World trip to know which rides are closed and what the community says about Genie+. Before I build anything to know what problems people are actually hitting.

If you're meeting with a CEO, have you read all their tweets and YouTube transcripts from the last 30 days? I have.

Sources, scored by the people

The unfiltered take. Top comments with real upvote counts, free, no API key. The real opinions that Google buries. With your OK, it can also search as your own logged-in Reddit account for more threads and live scores.
The hot take, the expert thread, the breaking reaction. First to know, first to argue.
The 45-minute deep dive. Full transcripts searched for the 5 quotable sentences that matter.
The creator reaching 3.6M people with a take you'll never find on Google.
The influencer perspective with spoken-word transcripts. The visual culture signal.
The developer consensus. 825 points, 899 comments. Where technical people actually argue.
Not opinions. Odds. Backed by real money. 96% confidence on album sales. 4% on an acquisition. The report puts a market's odds on one line under the story it bears on, with how much they moved.
For people: PR velocity, top repos by stars, release notes. For topics: issues and discussions.
Story clusters from every Digg topic (AI, tech, world and business, sports, science, gaming, entertainment), ranked by Digg Score, with attributable inline quotes from X (no X auth required). Auto-enabled when is on PATH. An older still works, on AI and tech only and without scores.
The papers behind the hype. New research in the window, free, no API key. Auto-enabled when is on PATH (first-run setup installs it).
The tech-news editorial layer, date-windowed to your 30 days. Free, no API key. Auto-enabled when is on PATH (first-run setup installs it).
The market's read on a company. The share-price move over your 30 days, next to the S&P 500 for US listings. Free, no API key. Shows when your topic is a listed company or the person who leads one and is on PATH (first-run setup installs it).
The professional signal. Posts and articles, with articles weighted as high signal.
What a brand is paying to say. Live Meta ad creatives launched this month, with copy, promo codes, and spoken transcripts.
Trader sentiment. Auto-activates when your topic is a ticker or crypto.
The post-Twitter text layer. Conversations from creators and brands.
Visual discovery. Pins, saves, and comments on products and ideas.
Chinese lifestyle, product, and creator signals. Requested explicitly with when a logged-in x-mcp browser plugin or service is running locally.
The decentralized social layer. AT Protocol posts from the post-Twitter migration.
Controlled Agent API synthesis, OpenRouter Sonar fallback, raw Search API rows, and explicit Deep Research.
Developer articles and top comments through the public, keyless API. Opt in with , , or .
Posts searched with ; available when authenticated.
Public posts from named channels. Opt-in; requires and a channel list. No keyword discovery.
Company TrustScore, review count, and an AI summary of customer feedback. Opt-in; requires on PATH and a usable session.
Product ratings, prices, and customer reviews. Opt-in; requires an authenticated CLI and uses your Bright Data credits.
Financial newsletters and analyst writeups through a public, keyless API. Opt in with or INCLUDE_SOURCES=dripstack.
What a company is hiring for, read from its own careers page (Workday, Apple, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Netflix, Oracle, and more). A company run reads it automatically, and roles that hint at something unannounced become Jobs Page Secret Signals. Also selected with , , or the research plan.
A company's new US patent filings, as evidence of what it is building before it ships. Free, no API key. Shows when your topic is a company. A filing becomes a Patent Secret Signal only when it is out of character for the company or describes something it has not shipped or announced.
Your local Markdown and text files, plus PDFs when is on PATH. Opt in with or .
The editorial coverage, the blog comparisons. One signal of many, not the only one.

Ask to include the sources you need. Availability depends on credentials, installed tools, the topic, and explicit opt-ins. See source requirements for configuration.

A Reddit thread with 1,500 upvotes is a stronger signal than a blog post nobody read. A TikTok with 3.6M views tells you more about what's culturally relevant than a press release. Polymarket odds backed by $66K in volume are harder to argue with than a pundit's guess.

The synthesis ranks by what real people actually engaged with. Social relevancy, not SEO relevancy.

What people actually use it for

/last30days Peter Steinberger - joined OpenAI's Codex team, fighting Anthropic's ban on third-party agents, 23 PRs merged at 85% merge rate on GitHub, building LobsterOS for cross-device agent control. r/ClaudeCode: "Ever since OpenClaw released, it was widely known that if you run it through anything other than the API, you were gonna get banned eventually" (227 upvotes). That's not on LinkedIn.

To see what a company is building before it ships. - the Jobs Page Secret Signal flagged a new director role testing whether requests trigger transactions that run through partner APIs and financial systems, which reads like quality control for an assistant that completes purchases. The Patent Secret Signal flagged an application for changing a device's state by tapping it in a saved photo of your room. Polymarket put Apple at 91% to be the world's largest company at year end. found a product manager role for "YouTube Ads Agentic Buyflows", and its stock line read down 17.6% over 30 days while the S&P 500 fell 3.6%, with the worst day on Oct 29 (-12.6%). For a hiring-only report, add .

To find the topic before it peaks. Ask /last30days what's exploding in AI agents? and the skill switches to discovery mode: the engine sweeps Reddit category listings, Hacker News front/best stories, Digg stories, and X when authenticated; your agent judges the nominations (names, junk filtering, content-worthiness) and writes podcast / X-article angles; then you get 5-10 velocity-ranked topics. Every result includes cross-source numbers, a momentum label, and a ready-to-run follow-up.

- UK blocked his visa, Wireless Festival canceled, sponsors fled. But BULLY debuted #2 on Billboard. Fantano came back from his "Yay sabbatical" to review it (653K views). SoFi Homecoming brought out Lauryn Hill and Travis Scott for 44 songs. Polymarket: "Will Kanye tweet again?" 86% Yes. 23 Reddit threads, 17 YouTube videos, 86K upvotes.

/last30days OpenClaw vs Hermes vs Paperclip - "These aren't competitors, they're layers." OpenClaw is the executor (351K GitHub stars, live), Hermes is the self-improving brain (31K stars), Paperclip is the org chart (49K stars). Star counts pulled live from the GitHub API, not stale blog posts. Side-by-side table with architecture, memory, security, best-for. Per @IMJustinBrooke: "OpenClaw = Charmander, Hermes = Charizard."

- Day 38 of the war. Trump's Tuesday deadline for Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Two US warplanes downed. Oil at $126/barrel. The IEA called it "the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market." Polymarket: ceasefire by Dec 31 at 74%. 27 X posts, 10 YouTube videos, 20 prediction markets.

/last30days Universal Epic Universe - Expansion already under construction. "Project 680" permit filed. Fireworks show confirmed by infrastructure but unannounced. Wait times: Mine-Cart Madness averaging 148 minutes. No annual pass yet, and locals are frustrated. Stardust Racers down for refurbishment through April 5.

/last30days Nano Banana Pro prompting - JSON-structured prompts are replacing tag soup. @pictsbyai's nested format prevents "concept bleeding." Edit-first workflow beats regeneration. Then it writes you a production prompt using exactly what the community said works.

v4 reads what a company is doing before it announces it, and makes every report easier to quote:

  • Patent Secret Signals: a company run reads that month's US patent filings, with no key, and flags only the ones that are out of character or describe something unannounced.
  • Jobs Page Secret Signals: it reads the company's own careers page and flags the roles that give away what's coming, including new teams nobody has covered yet.
  • Quote lines: the best Reddit, X, YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram comments sit on their own line under the story they back up, translated when needed, and a line said in a video can be quoted too.
  • Polymarket odds line: one line under the story it bears on, with how much the odds moved.
  • Yahoo Finance line: a listed company's share price over the last 30 days next to the S&P 500, plus its biggest single-day move.
  • Knows who you mean: "Apple" resolves to the company, its site, and its ticker on its own.
  • Reddit as you: with your OK, Reddit searches as your own logged-in account.
  • Digg covers every topic now, not just AI and tech.

This README describes the current source tree; your installed version may differ.

grok plugin marketplace add mvanhorn/last30days-skill then grok plugin install last30daysgrok plugin update last30days

Grok Build () installs last30days as a native plugin. Direct install tracks the repository:

Or add this repo as a marketplace source, then install by plugin name:

grok plugin marketplace add mvanhorn/last30days-skill

On Grok Bot, where last30days installs from the marketplace, X works out of the box through the bot's built-in X tools, then the bot's X connector, with the official X API () as backup.

Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other Agent Skills hosts

Install via the open Agent Skills CLI — supports 50+ harnesses including , , , , , , , , , , , , and more (full list on the vercel-labs/skills repo).

npx skills add mvanhorn/last30days-skill -g

The (global) flag installs to your user directory so the skill is available across all projects. Without , installs project-locally into (committed with the repo). For a research-the-world tool, global is what you want.

Codex desktop and other folder-mode hosts can work in ordinary folders as well as Git repos. To inspect what a run would read and write without starting research, run the bundled scripts/last30days.py --preflight from the loaded skill directory; in a source checkout, the equivalent command is python3 skills/last30days/scripts/last30days.py --preflight. It shows the config source, browser-cookie plan, planned writes, optional commands, and ignored project config without reading cookies, writing files, or running research. First-run setup does not require it.

By default this installs for whichever harness detects. To target a specific one (or multiple):

npx skills add mvanhorn/last30days-skill -g -a codex
npx skills add mvanhorn/last30days-skill -g -a cursor
npx skills add mvanhorn/last30days-skill -g -a gemini-cli
